product_from_film: Grade ties creator and other worker payments to measured performance.
explains_well: A rate field leads to creator performance cards and payment confirmations, making the payment idea visible.
unclear: The shown $4 per 1,000 views does not explain the following 25K-view/$1,000 payout example; the film may be switching examples without saying so.
scenario: Compare creator reach, set a view-based rate, pay creators, then extend the idea to commissions and recruitment fees.
product_clear_basis: The Grade identity is followed by a $4 per 1,000 views rate field at 28–29s.

categories.finding: Unequal reach/equal pay → waste → performance rate → creator payouts → other commissions → payroll ambition.
A seated presenter appears and phone clips join him; the opening question depends on speech draft support.
Marketers paying creators are the initial audience; the film later broadens to performance payroll. The rate form makes the mechanism clear at 28s.
Cards multiply, values change, cursors approach payment buttons and oversized text changes scale/position. Exact transitions/easing are unverified.
Presenter shots alternate with white/green graphic demonstrations. Repeated card grids carry the payroll idea across roles.
Dark warm interview footage contrasts with clean green and white graphic fields.
Rate and payout labels carry essential meaning. Full frames at 28–30s show $4/1,000 views followed by 25K views/$1,000; a changed rate or other basis is not stated.
ASR supports a question, problem argument, demo explanation and market ambition; delivery and sound design remain unknown.

categories.finding: Rate setting and payment states are visible, but the equal-pay twist and auto-tracking claim rely on speech support.
Large figures anchor each argument; green buttons and payout amounts guide the demo. Multiple simultaneous cards reduce attention to one calculation.
The central creator demo occupies about 10s before expanding into global reach and other job types. A single calculation deserves a hold.
Different views lead to different payouts, answering the opening value question in principle. The displayed rate-to-payout math is unclear.
The opening question/reversal suggests surprise, then payment confirmations suggest control; viewer response is unmeasured.
Green/white styling and worker cards unify the roles, but no initial creator is clearly tracked through the final payout.
Market size, waste, automatic tracking, reach and payment claims are unverified. The numerical discontinuity is a film explanation issue, not a verified product defect.
The rate-per-view form gives Grade specificity; broad future-of-work text is less distinctive.
Use one mathematically consistent example.
categories.experiment: Keep a creator visible while $4 × 25 thousand views produces $100, then show the matching payment result or explain any added basis.
